numbers.headline: Of Americans who had ever been hooked on nicotine, nearly 1 in 5 had no signs of it left when asked.
numbers.mirror: You think nobody hooked like you ever really gets free.

basis.design: national survey (NESARC), face-to-face interviews, one snapshot
basis.who: US adults who had ever met the criteria for nicotine dependence (3 of 7 signs within one year), from any tobacco, before vaping was common
basis.n: 1,300 who were free, of 6,937 ever hooked (unweighted counts from the paper's tables; 43,093 adults surveyed)
basis.measured: Whether, by the interview, the person had finally stopped having any sign of being hooked, with none coming back, as they recalled it. 18.7% is 1,300 divided by 6,937.

numbers.caveat: A snapshot: many had been hooked only a few years when asked, so it is not a lifetime share. 'Free' means no signs of being hooked left, not always nicotine-free. People in prison or hospital were not asked.
numbers.weak: The tables give the 1,300 without saying in words what it counts; it is read as those who had got free. Unweighted, so not exactly the national share.

ref.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Hasin DS, de los Cobos JP, Pines A, Wang S, Grant BF, Blanco C (2011). Probability and predictors of remission from life-time nicotine, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine dependence: results from the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions. Addiction 106(3):657-69.
ref.quote: lifetime history of dependence on nicotine (n=6,937) … Nicotine remission (N=1,300)

numbers.origin: new (the N=1,300 table header was noted as unclear in 07-mirror-stats/lq-details.json; read from Tables 3 and 4 of the full text, refetched from PMC on 2026-11-05)

numbers.headline: 83.7% of Americans ever hooked on nicotine are projected to get free of it in their lifetime.
numbers.mirror: You've smoked so long you think it's too late for you.

basis.design: national survey (NESARC), face-to-face interviews; ages recalled and modelled over a lifetime (standard life-table model)
basis.who: US adults who had ever met the criteria for nicotine dependence (3 of 7 signs within one year), from any tobacco, before vaping was common
basis.measured: The age when the signs first appeared and the age when they finally stopped and never came back, as people recalled it. From those ages the model projects the share free over a whole life. 3.0% were free within a year of getting hooked and 18.4% within 10 years.

numbers.caveat: 'Free' means no signs of being hooked left, not that they never touched it again. Men got free less often than women. People in prison or hospital, and people who died, weren't surveyed, so the true share is likely lower.
numbers.weak: A projection, not a count, and likely high: people in prison or hospital and people who died were not asked.

ref.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Hasin DS, de los Cobos JP, Pines A, Wang S, Grant BF, Blanco C (2011). Probability and predictors of remission from life-time nicotine, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine dependence: results from the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions. Addiction 106(3):657-69.
ref.quote: Lifetime cumulative probability estimates of dependence remission were 83.7% for nicotine

numbers.origin: 06-template.json nicotine hero '83.7%' (basis as in 07-mirror-stats/lq-details.json; quote cut before the other substances, rule 13)

numbers.headline: For daily smokers in Ontario, the best estimate was about 30 quit tries, on average, before one lasted a year.
numbers.mirror: You've quit a hundred times and think you're the exception.
numbers.counted: daily smokers who tried to quit, not checked for addiction

basis.design: cohort surveyed every 6 months for up to 3 years; tries turned into tries-per-success with a life table
basis.who: adult daily smokers in Ontario who made a quit try during follow-up
basis.n: 1,092 daily smokers (of 1,277 smokers who tried to quit)
basis.measured: Quit tries, and quits that lasted a year or more, during follow-up. The authors' preferred model gave 29.5 for daily smokers (29.6 for everyone). Other ways of counting gave about 7, 20 and 142. The first try had the best odds of lasting (11%).

numbers.caveat: An average from a model, pulled up by the people who struggle most; it is not what every smoker needs. Self-report, cigarette smokers only.
numbers.weak: Daily smokers, not checked for addiction, and the answer swings from about 7 to 142 depending on the model's assumptions.

ref.cite: Chaiton M, Diemert L, Cohen JE, et al. (2016). Estimating the number of quit attempts it takes to quit smoking successfully in a longitudinal cohort of smokers. BMJ Open.
ref.quote: Overall (n=1277) | Daily (n=1092) | Occasional (n=185) … Life table, observed quit success rates … 29.6 | 29.5 | 11.4

numbers.origin: 07-mirror-stats/nicotine.json how 'About 30' (same source; the daily-smoker column of Table 3 used so the group can carry the 'heavy' tag; refetched from PMC on 2026-11-05)

numbers.headline: Only 3–5% of unaided quit tries lasted six months to a year; most slips came in the first eight days.
numbers.mirror: You slipped within days and think it proves you can't quit.
numbers.counted: smokers trying to quit on their own, not checked for addiction

basis.design: systematic review (too few, too mixed studies to pool)
basis.who: smokers trying to quit without treatment
basis.n: 15 studies or study groups (a summary of 10 earlier studies, 2 more studies and 3 untreated groups); the review didn't add up the people
basis.where: The review doesn't list the countries
basis.measured: Share still not smoking 6 to 12 months after one quit attempt, and when relapse happens (8 relapse curves).

numbers.caveat: This is per attempt, not per person: many people try again and succeed later.
numbers.weak: The smokers in these studies were not checked for addiction, and the studies are old and too mixed to pool.

ref.cite: Hughes JR, Keely J, Naud S (2004). Shape of the relapse curve and long-term abstinence among untreated smokers. Addiction.
ref.quote: 3-5% of self-quitters achieve prolonged abstinence for 6-12 month after a given quit attempt.

numbers.origin: 07-mirror-stats/nicotine.json quit '3–5%' (figure, basis and ref kept; the owner liked this 'How quitting goes' number, rule 26; see the gap note on its severity tag)

numbers.headline: Across 22 trials, cutting down first and then stopping worked about as well as stopping all at once.
numbers.mirror: You can't face stopping all at once, so you never start.
numbers.counted: smokers in quit trials who wanted to stop

basis.design: Cochrane review; this figure pools 22 randomised trials
basis.who: adults who smoke and want to quit, about 23 cigarettes a day on average
basis.n: 9,219 people in 22 trials (of 51 trials with 22,509 people in the review)
basis.where: 29 of the review's 51 trials in the USA, most others in Europe and China; most recruited volunteers through ads
basis.measured: Not smoking at 6 months or longer: a plan to cut down before quitting, against quitting on a set day. Cutting down with varenicline or fast nicotine (gum, spray) may work better than cutting down alone.

numbers.caveat: Cutting down here is a step on the way to stopping, not smoking less for good. Moderate certainty. One large English trial (697 smokers, all given nicotine replacement and nurse support) found stopping at once did better: 22.0% against 15.5% still off at 6 months.

ref.cite: Lindson N, Klemperer E, Hong B, Ordóñez-Mena JM, Aveyard P (2019). Smoking reduction interventions for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.
ref.quote: There is moderate-certainty evidence that neither reduction-to-quit nor abrupt quitting interventions result in superior long-term quit rates when compared with one another.

numbers.origin: 07-mirror-stats/nicotine.json works 'About equal' (figure, basis and ref kept; caveat adds that cutting down here leads to stopping)

numbers.headline: On varenicline, 23 in 100 smokers stayed off cigarettes six months or more; on a dummy pill, 10 in 100.
numbers.mirror: You think quit pills are for weak people.
numbers.counted: smokers in quit trials who wanted to stop

basis.design: Cochrane review, 41 randomised trials for this comparison
basis.who: adult smokers who wanted to stop
basis.where: of the review's 75 trials, 28 in the USA; others in Canada, Europe, Asia and Australia, some across several countries
basis.measured: Not smoking at 6 months or longer, checked by breath or blood test where possible; varenicline against a dummy pill. 23 in 100 is the review's 230 per 1,000; 10 in 100 rounds its 99 per 1,000. As a ratio: 2.32 times.

numbers.caveat: Prescription only. Serious side effects were reported a little more often than on a dummy pill (×1.23). Mostly tested in cigarette smokers, not vapers. It still leaves most people smoking at six months.

ref.cite: Livingstone-Banks J, Fanshawe TR, Thomas KH, et al. (2023). Nicotine receptor partial agonists for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.
ref.quote: Smoking abstinence at longest follow‐up (6+ months)(varenicline vs placebo) | 99 per 1000 | 230 per 1000(213 to 249) | RR 2.32(2.15 to 2.51)

numbers.origin: 07-mirror-stats/nicotine.json works '×2.3' (same review and comparison; figure re-expressed per 100 from its summary-of-findings table, full text refetched from PMC on 2026-11-05)

numbers.headline: One-to-one counselling: 10 to 12 in 100 smokers stay off six months, against seven in a hundred with brief advice.
numbers.mirror: You think talking to someone about smoking won't change anything.
numbers.counted: smokers in quit trials, no quit medicine offered

basis.design: Cochrane review; this figure pools 27 randomised trials
basis.who: adult smokers in trials where no one was offered quit medicine
basis.n: 11,100 people in 27 trials (of 49 trials, about 19,000 people, in the review)
basis.where: The review's short version does not list the countries
basis.measured: Not smoking at least six months later: face-to-face counselling of 10 minutes or more (most much longer, many with follow-up calls) against brief advice, usual care or leaflets. As a ratio: 1.57 times.

numbers.caveat: The 7 in 100 is the review's own example of a typical brief-advice group, not one measured rate. When everyone also had nicotine replacement, counselling added less (ratio 1.24).

ref.cite: Lancaster T, Stead LF (2017). Individual behavioural counselling for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.
ref.quote: if seven out of 100 smokers managed to quit for at least six months … then between 10 and 12 in 100 would be expected to be successful after having counselling

numbers.headline: In people hooked on nicotine who stayed off, anxiety began to fall in the first week.
numbers.mirror: You think quitting will leave you on edge for weeks.
numbers.counted: people hooked on nicotine who stayed off four weeks

basis.design: quit-smoking trial (authors at St George's Hospital Medical School, London); anxiety rated before and after quit day
basis.who: smokers who met the criteria for nicotine dependence (DSM-III-R) and tried to stop
basis.n: 70 who stayed off for all 4 weeks (of 101 who tried)
basis.measured: Anxiety by a single rating and a standard anxiety questionnaire (State-Trait Anxiety Inventory), from 2 weeks before quit day to 4 weeks after. Only people with no slip at all counted as off.

numbers.caveat: It shows anxiety fell in those who stayed off, not how much. People who slipped are not in this count. They were in a quit trial, so may have had support or medicine.
numbers.weak: Small: 70 people in one trial from the 1990s, and the size of the fall is not stated in the paper's short version.

ref.cite: West R, Hajek P (1997). What happens to anxiety levels on giving up smoking? American Journal of Psychiatry 154(11):1589-92.
ref.quote: Seventy patients were abstinent for the 4-week follow-up period. … However, there was a significant decrease in anxiety from the first week of abstinence.

numbers.headline: Smokers in a quit trial who quit rated life and mood better than those still smoking, one and three years on.
numbers.mirror: You worry life will feel empty without cigarettes.
numbers.counted: smokers in a quit trial, followed three years

basis.design: cohort within a randomised quit-smoking trial, followed 3 years
basis.n: 376 quitters vs 649 smokers at year 1; 359 vs 640 at year 3 (1,504 started)
basis.measured: Quality of life, health-related quality of life, mood, relationship satisfaction and stressful events; smoking checked by a biochemical test. Quitters also had fewer stressors by year 3.

numbers.caveat: Quitters weren't chosen at random, so they may differ in other ways. Overall life rating slipped a little for everyone, but less for quitters. Marriage satisfaction did not change.
numbers.weak: It shows a direction, not a size: no plain number says how much better life got.

ref.cite: Piper ME, Kenford S, Fiore MC, Baker TB (2012). Smoking cessation and quality of life: changes in life satisfaction over 3 years following a quit attempt. Annals of Behavioral Medicine.
ref.quote: Compared with continuing smokers, quitters showed improved global QOL, HR-QOL, and affect at years 1 and 3 and fewer stressors by year 3.

numbers.origin: 07-mirror-stats/nicotine.json after 'Years 1 and 3' (figure, basis, caveat and ref kept)

numbers.headline: Half of Americans ever hooked on nicotine are projected to be free about 26 years after it began.
numbers.mirror: You've smoked since your teens and think you're a lifer.

basis.design: national survey (NESARC), face-to-face interviews; ages recalled and modelled over a lifetime
basis.who: adults who had ever been dependent on nicotine
basis.n: 6,937 adults who had ever been hooked (of 43,093 surveyed); 1,300 of them had got free
basis.measured: The age when the signs of being hooked first appeared, and the age when they finally stopped and never came back, as people recalled it. Getting free here means no signs of being hooked any more; it does not have to mean never using. 3.0% got free within the first year and 18.4% within 10 years.

numbers.caveat: The study projects that 83.7% get free at some point in life; that is a model, not a head count. People in prisons or hospitals weren't surveyed, so the real pace may be slower. Men got free more slowly than women. Mostly cigarette smokers, before vaping.
numbers.weak: A projection from ages people recalled over decades; people in prison or hospital were not asked, so the real wait may be longer.

ref.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Hasin DS, de los Cobos JP, Pines A, Wang S, Grant BF, Blanco C (2011). Probability and predictors of remission from life-time nicotine, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine dependence: results from the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions. Addiction 106(3):657-69.
ref.quote: Half of the cases of nicotine … dependence remitted approximately 26 … years after dependence onset

numbers.origin: 07-mirror-stats/nicotine.json who '26 years' (headline marked as projected; the other substances removed from line, basis and quote, rule 13)

numbers.headline: With rewards for staying off, 10 in 100 smokers in trials were off six months later; without, 7 in 100.
numbers.mirror: You'd quit faster if something real was on the line.
numbers.counted: smokers in quit trials, rewarded for staying off

basis.design: Cochrane review; this figure pools 39 randomised trials
basis.who: adults who smoke (not pregnant), in workplaces, clinics and communities
basis.where: 33 of the review's 48 trials were in the USA, most others in Europe
basis.measured: Not smoking at the last check, 6 months or later: cash, vouchers, or money people put down themselves and won back, against no rewards. As a ratio: 1.52 times. Leaving out trials still paying at that check: 1.46 times, so the gain lasted after rewards stopped.

numbers.caveat: In most trials a program ran the rewards and checked people's breath or urine. A private bet with a friend was not what was tested.

ref.cite: Notley C, Gentry S, Livingstone-Banks J, Bauld L, Perera R, Conde M, Hartmann-Boyce J (2025). Incentives for smoking cessation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.
ref.quote: For every 100 people who received financial incentives, 10 people were likely to successfully quit smoking at six months or longer, compared to 7 in 100

numbers.origin: 07-mirror-stats/nicotine.json works '×1.5' (same review; figure re-expressed per 100 from its plain-language summary for rule 12a, full text refetched from PMC on 2026-11-05)

numbers.headline: People who stayed quit gained 4–5 kg on average in the first year, most of it in three months.
numbers.mirror: You're afraid quitting will make you fat.
numbers.counted: people who stayed quit in quit trials

basis.who: people who stayed quit in quit-smoking trials, with or without medication
basis.n: 514 quitters without medication at 12 months, in 25 studies (1,138 more on nicotine replacement)
basis.where: 59 of 62 trials in North America, Europe or Australia
basis.measured: Weight change from quit day to 1, 2, 3, 6 and 12 months. At 12 months: 16% lost weight, 37% gained under 5 kg, 34% gained 5–10 kg, 13% gained over 10 kg.

numbers.caveat: An average; it varies a lot between people. Measured in cigarette smokers in trials, not in vapers.

ref.cite: Aubin HJ, Farley A, Lycett D, Lahmek P, Aveyard P (2012). Weight gain in smokers after quitting cigarettes: meta-analysis. BMJ.
ref.quote: Smoking cessation is associated with a mean increase of 4-5 kg in body weight after 12 months of abstinence, and most weight gain occurs within three months of quitting.

numbers.origin: 07-mirror-stats/nicotine.json after '4–5 kg' (figure, basis and ref kept)

gaps.searched: Europe PMC and web searches for the mean or median age when nicotine dependence ended ('age at remission', 'mean age' with remission, recovery, ex-smokers). Read in full: Lopez-Quintero 2011 (NESARC, PMC3227547), Dierker 2008 (NCS-R, PMC2659851), Goodwin 2011 (NESARC, PMC3337717), Chou 2016 (NESARC-III, PMC8154113).
gaps.why: None reports an average or median age when nicotine dependence ended. Lopez-Quintero gives years from getting hooked to getting free (a median of about 26), not the age. Ages at quitting exist for ex-smokers in general, but those count ordinary smokers, which rule 3 bans in the who-gets-free group. The National Recovery Survey behind the alcohol 'about 38' did not ask about nicotine. Later: our r/stopsmoking harvest could give a self-hooked count of age at quitting from posts that state both age and quit date.

gaps.searched: Europe PMC and web searches for untreated or unassisted remission among people who had been nicotine-dependent (NESARC, NCS-R, 'natural recovery', 'formal help', 'without treatment'). Read: Lopez-Quintero 2011 (no treatment data), Chou 2016 NESARC-III, Smith 2015 (07).
gaps.why: No source counts, among people who were hooked on nicotine and got free, how many never used treatment, a group or medicine. Nearest: Chou 2016 (NESARC-III) found 18.8% of everyone ever hooked had ever used any treatment (27.8% of severe cases), but that counts everyone ever hooked, mild included, not only those who got free, so using it would stretch it. The 07 Australian review (54–69% of ex-smokers quit unassisted) counts ordinary ex-smokers, tag 'users', which kinds.json does not allow here. Later: our r/stopsmoking harvest could count quit posts naming cold turkey against patches, pills or vapes (self-hooked).

gaps.searched: Filled with the owner-liked 07 number (Hughes 2004, 3–5%). Looked for the populations of the studies it pools; the full text is behind a paywall (Wiley returned 403). Looked for a slip-and-when number in a dependent group: West and Hajek 1997 (31 of 101 dependent smokers slipped within 4 weeks, one small trial) and NESARC papers (relapse among ex-smokers in general).
gaps.why: Not empty, but flagged: the smokers in Hughes 2004 were not checked for addiction, so the honest tag is 'users', which kinds.json does not allow for how-slips and the build will reject. Rule 26 says keep the 'How quitting goes' numbers he liked, and this is the nicotine one. Decision needed: allow 'users' for how-slips with the tag shown, or swap in a smaller dependent-group number.

notUsed.reason: Share of US 18-to-24-year-olds who vape: ordinary users, a prevalence figure that answers no kind on the menu.
Smokers who want to stop and tried in the past year: ordinary smokers, and no kind on the menu asks it.
Projected share of first-time smokers who get hooked: about how it starts, no kind on the menu.
Teens losing control within days of first inhaling: about how it starts, teens only, no kind on the menu.
Odds of erection problems in smokers: a cost of smoking in ordinary smokers aged 40+, no cost kind on the menu.
Weekly spend of smokers in England: ordinary users; after-first-month does not allow the 'users' tag.
Less sleep in current smokers than never-smokers: ordinary users compared at one night, not a change after quitting; after-sleep is not picked.
Erections improved in at least 1 in 4 men who quit: after-body is not picked and holds the larger weight number; this one is 118 men in one clinic. Candidate if he wants sex over weight on the page.
Quit ratio among everyone who ever smoked 100 cigarettes: ordinary smokers, which rule 3 bans in the hope group; the counted dependent figure is used instead.
Ex-smokers who quit unassisted (Australia): ordinary ex-smokers, tag 'users', not allowed for how-alone; see the how-alone gap.
Unplanned quit tries lasted longer: no kind on the menu asks planned against unplanned, and it counts ordinary smokers.
Methods smokers used on their last try: what people use, not what works, among current smokers (tag 'users'), which how-abrupt does not allow.
Vapes beat patches or gum for getting off cigarettes: a switch, not an exit; helps-medicine takes the best-tested quit medicine, varenicline.
Varenicline for quitting vaping: 2 small trials, low certainty; helps-medicine takes the 41-trial smoking figure. Candidate for a vape-only line later.
Nicotine replacement against placebo: weaker than varenicline, which fills helps-medicine; one number per kind.

alternatives.note: A second head count from the same survey, looser test: of adults ever hooked at the first interview (2001–02), 48.9% no longer met the criteria for nicotine dependence in the year before the second (2004–05). Not used: it allows some signs to remain, its two n's disagree (5,256 ever hooked, but 2,793 + 2,903 = 5,696), and a jump from about 28% not currently hooked at the first interview to about half three years later looks too fast against a median of 26 years, so the stricter 1 in 5 goes first (rule 10).

ref.cite: Goodwin RD, Pagura J, Spiwak R, Lemeshow AR, Sareen J (2011). Predictors of persistent nicotine dependence among adults in the United States. Drug and Alcohol Dependence 118:127-33.
ref.quote: At Wave 2, 48.9% of the sample (n=2793) no longer met criteria for nicotine dependence, while 51.1% of the sample (n=2903) had persistent nicotine dependence
